findings.title: Classical signature (RSA-2048): future quantum risk
findings.detail: The server proves its identity with RSA-2048, which a quantum computer will be able to forge. This is not "harvest now, decrypt later": a signature only has to hold during the handshake, so the risk starts the day such a computer exists, not before. It does not limit today's security grade; in quantum readiness (model 2026.3), a post-quantum certificate would add 15 points.
findings.remediation: Nothing to do on the signature yet. Automate renewal (ACME) so you can switch to post-quantum (ML-DSA or hybrid) certificates as soon as authorities issue them: today this certificate shows no sign of renewing itself.

findings.title: No sign of automated renewal
findings.detail: 90-day validity, issued by QuantumReady TLS lab. Maximum certificate validity is already 200 days (since 15 March 2026) and will drop to 100 days on 15 March 2027 and to 47 on 15 March 2029 (CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081). Moving to post-quantum certificates will require reissuing them: without automation, every change is manual work and an expiry risk.
findings.remediation: Automate issuance and renewal with ACME (certbot, Caddy, cert-manager…), with your current authority if it supports it or a free one.

findings.title: CCM_8 suites (64-bit tag)
findings.detail: CCM_8 is authenticated encryption with a 64-bit integrity tag instead of 128, meant for very constrained devices. It is not broken, but it leaves less margin than AES-GCM and makes no sense on a website. Suites: TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256 (TLS 1.3).
findings.remediation: Disable them unless an embedded client needs them.

findings.title: Pure ML-KEM accepted: MLKEM768, MLKEM1024
findings.detail: The server accepts ML-KEM without a classical component (FIPS 203). The NSA prefers it that way for national security systems (CNSA 2.0), but browsers use the hybrids, so it counts towards post-quantum group variety, not towards key exchange.

findings.title: AES-128 and Grover's algorithm
findings.detail: The connection uses TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256. In theory Grover's algorithm reduces AES-128 to about 64-bit security, but it does not parallelize in practice and NIST still considers AES-128 adequate. Informational: it neither adds nor takes away on either axis.

findings.title: No transparency SCTs
findings.detail: No SCTs were found (neither embedded nor in the handshake). Browsers require them for public certificates, so this usually means a private certificate. Informational.

findings.title: Other groups accepted: brainpoolP256r1tls13, ffdhe2048, ffdhe3072
findings.detail: Valid but uncommon classical groups (ffdhe, brainpool, x448…). Informational: never scored.

findings.title: Post-quantum key exchange: X25519MLKEM768
findings.detail: With a current browser's offer, the server negotiates the hybrid group X25519MLKEM768 (classical + ML-KEM, FIPS 203). Traffic captured today stays protected even if a quantum computer breaks the classical part ("harvest now, decrypt later").

findings.title: Several standard post-quantum groups: X25519MLKEM768, MLKEM768, MLKEM1024
findings.detail: Besides the group browsers use, the server accepts other standard ML-KEM groups, useful for clients with other requirements (FIPS, CNSA 2.0).

findings.title: TLS 1.3 available
findings.detail: TLS 1.3 is the current protocol version and the only one where hybrid post-quantum groups exist.

findings.title: Valid certificate
findings.detail: The chain is trusted, matches the name and is current (issuer: QuantumReady TLS lab; expires in 46 days).

findings.title: Forward secrecy
findings.detail: Every connection uses an ephemeral key exchange: even if the server's private key leaked, it would not decrypt past connections.

not_evaluated.label: PSK, SRP, Kerberos and GOST suites (they need credentials or algorithms a scanner does not have)
